papers.title_in_file: Hardware-efficient variational quantum algorithms for time evolution
papers.version_note: The text is arXiv:2009.12361v5, dated July 22, 2021 (arXiv stamp 27 Jul 2021). The text layer holds the paper once. Page numbers below count the page-number markers in the text layer as the top of each page; the stored anchors for the Discussion say p. 8, but in this layer those two sentences sit before the page-8 marker.
papers.what_it_is: A variational quantum simulation paper that replaces the matrix-inversion step of the time-dependent variational principle with Trotterized, causal-cone, coordinatewise update rules (cone, block and angle update), tested by exact classical simulation on small quantum Ising chains.

existing.note: The sentence about angle update is stated as in the stored value. The second half is limited by Sec. III C: cone update converges to the optimal objective value of one only for the four-qubit causal cone, block and angle update do not benefit from more sweeps, and for the six-qubit cone no method reaches one. The ground-state evidence is exact simulation of small quantum Ising chains (Figs. 1 and 7), where all three methods reach similar low energies for the chosen time step. The stored page anchor (p. 8) is p. 7 in this text layer.
existing.value: The authors state that angle update, their most efficient algorithm, performed remarkably well at finding ground states by imaginary time evolution, and that they presented numerical evidence that block and cone update achieve the high accuracy required for real time evolution. In Sec. III C they report that cone update converges to the optimal objective value of one for the four-qubit causal cone while block and angle update do not benefit from an increased number of sweeps, that none of the methods converge to the optimal value of one in the six-qubit case, and that for imaginary time evolution on the quantum Ising chain all methods reach similar low energies for their choice of time step.

existing.note: Confirmed as to the claim, with one limit the value omits: every numerical result is from classical simulation in which expectations and Hadamard tests are calculated exactly, with no finite-sampling noise and no hardware noise (Appendix G).
existing.value: The authors present alternatives to the time-dependent variational principle that are hardware-efficient and do not require matrix inversion, and analyze them numerically on quantum Hamiltonians with local interactions. The numerical simulations calculate expectations and Hadamard tests exactly and include no finite-sampling noise or hardware noise.
quotes: Here we present alternatives to the time-dependent variational principle that are hardware-eﬃcient and do not require matrix inversion.
We numerically analyze the performance of our algorithms using quantum Hamiltonians with local interactions.
Expectations and Hadamard tests are calculated exactly. We do not include ﬁnite-sampling noise or hardware noise.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; the numerical analysis is classical and noise-free.

assertions.value: The authors define, for this work, a hardware-efficient variational quantum algorithm as any such algorithm that either (i) can use parameterized quantum circuits tailored to the physical device or (ii) exploits other concepts that reduce the number of qubits or gates, such as causal cones.
quotes: In this work, we call hardware-eﬃcient any variational quantum algorithm that (i) can use parameterized quantum circuits tailored to the physical device [42] or (ii) exploits other concepts that reduce the number of qubits or gates [43, 44] such as causal cones.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition of the term in Sec. I.

assertions.value: The authors state that the expectation of an operator acting on a few qubits depends only on the blocks inside its causal cone, and that for a two-qubit operator the expectation can be estimated with a quantum circuit of six qubits and five blocks regardless of the overall size of the PQC Ansatz. They state that the number of required physical qubits depends only on the depth of the Ansatz and on the Trotter term.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II B, p. 2 and p. 3
quotes: An interesting property is that the expectation of an operator acting on a few qubits depends only on the blocks inside its causal cone.
The expectation can be estimated with a quantum circuit of six qubits and ﬁve blocks, regardless of the overall size of the PQC Ansätze.
of the Ansatz and on the Trotter term.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without derivation in the paper; the six-qubit figure holds for the depth D = 2 Ansatz used throughout.
assertions.reader_inference: The qubit count depends on the depth, so the six-qubit figure is specific to the depth-2 Ansatz of Fig. 3 (a); the paper also says it uses depth 2 throughout.

assertions.value: The authors state that the variational algorithm requires only the preparation of circuits on quantum hardware of a size restricted by the causal cone, which allows variational states larger than the size allowed by the quantum computer. They state that periodic boundary conditions can be included with no additional hardware requirements and that the corresponding physical qubit-to-qubit connectivity is not required when using causal cones.

periodic boundary conditions can be included with no

assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the experiments are classical simulations that use causal cones to reduce the simulation size.

assertions.value: The authors state that for long-range operators, or operators acting on more than two qubits, one can obtain several causal cones.

one can obtain several causal cones.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement without derivation or experiment; all experiments use one- and two-qubit nearest-neighbor terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that throughout the paper they use the Ansatz of Fig. 3 (a) with the first nontrivial depth D = 2, and that each two-qubit block uses three CNOTs and Np = 15 adjustable parameters, a construction universal for two-qubit unitaries up to a global phase.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II B, p. 3; Appendix G, Fig. 10, p. 14
quotes: Throughout this paper we consider the Ansatz in Fig. 3 (a) with the ﬁrst nontrivial depth D = 2.
Each block has three CNOTs and Np = 15 adjustable parameters consisting of angles of rotation about the canonical x and z axes.
This construction has Np = 15 parameters and is universal for two-qubit unitaries up to a global phase.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own Ansatz depth and block construction in Sec. II B and Appendix G.

assertions.value: The authors state that the performance of their algorithms could be systematically improved by successively increasing the depth D, and that when the variational error becomes too large during the time evolution a new column of blocks initialized to 1 can be included at the end of the PQC to increase its expressive power.
quotes: The performance of our algorithms could be systematically improved by successively increasing the depth D.
we can include a new column of blocks initialized to 1 at the end of the PQC to increase its expressive power.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposal stated without an experiment; every experiment uses depth D = 2.

assertions.value: The paper shows that for a PQC with fixed gates and gates exp(−iθdGd), where Gd is Hermitian and unitary, the coordinatewise objective (the real part of the trace of an observable, a PQC applied to the initial state, and a fixed circuit) is a sinusoid in a single parameter with the others fixed, with amplitude A, phase B and a period, so its maximum can be found in closed form without the gradient or the Hessian.

assertions.value: The paper gives a closed-form coordinatewise update that sets a parameter to the maximizer of its sinusoidal objective, computed with the arctan2 function from objective evaluations at two parameter values a quarter period (π/2) apart, and states that the arctan2 function must be used to handle the sign of numerator and denominator and the case of a zero denominator. It states that the procedure sets the parameter to a value in (−π, π].

In practice, we choose k such that θd∗ ∈ (−π, π].

assertions.reader_inference: The quarter-period spacing is shown in Fig. 9 and Eq. (B3); the quotes here carry the stated implementation condition.

assertions.value: The paper shows that, in cone update, the objective value at the current parameter equals the amplitude found at the previous parameter update, so each parameter update needs a single new evaluation of the objective instead of two.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Eqs. (C1)-(C2), pp. 10-11; Sec. II C, p. 4
quotes: recycle information from previous steps and use a single evaluation.
At no additional cost, we calculate
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix C derives the recycling from the sinusoidal form, for the case where the objective does not change between updates.
assertions.reader_inference: Appendix E states this recycling cannot be done exactly in angle update, because the objective changes after each parameter update.

assertions.value: The authors define cone update as optimizing only the blocks in the causal cone of the Trotter term, with each Hadamard test requiring a number of controlled gates of order the product of the number of blocks in the causal cone and the number of parameters in a block.
quotes: We call this approach the cone update.
Hadamard test requires O(NbNp) controlled gates where Nb is the number of blocks in the causal cone, and Np is the number of parameters in a block.
assertions.certainty_reason: Defined in Sec. II D.

assertions.value: The authors define block update as replacing the previous variational state in the objective with the current variational state after a block has been updated, so that the two circuits differ by order Np parameters. For real time evolution it uses a time step τ /Nb in the objective, and the division is not necessary when τ is a hyperparameter, as in imaginary time evolution.
quotes: with the current variational state |ψ(θ) after a block has been updated.
Hence, to eﬀectively simulate time step τ we use a time step τ /Nb in the objective.
We call this approach the block update.
assertions.certainty_reason: Defined in Sec. II D.

assertions.value: The authors define angle update as replacing the previous variational state in the objective with the current variational state after an angle has been updated, so that the two circuits differ by one parameter at all times. For real time evolution it uses a time step τ /(NbNp) in the objective, since the replacement is done NbNp times.
quotes: The second level of approximation consists of replacing |ψk−1 in the objective with |ψ(θ) after an angle has been updated.
This guarantees that U and V diﬀer by one parameter at all times.
Since the replacement is done NbNp times, we use a time step τ /(NbNp) in the objective.
assertions.certainty_reason: Defined in Sec. II D.

assertions.value: The authors describe a Hadamard test with one ancilla qubit in which only the local differences between the two circuits are applied as gates controlled by the ancilla, so the ancilla subspaces hold the two states. The real part comes from the expectation of a Pauli Z on the ancilla times the Hamiltonian term, the imaginary part from the same procedure with a phase gate after the first Hadamard gate, and the test requires a number of controlled operations of order the number of blocks times the parameters per block.
assertions.anchor: Appendix D, p. 11; Sec. II D, p. 4
quotes: only locally to simplify the Hadamard test.
For the imaginary part, we follow the same procedure, but we include a phase gate after the ﬁrst Hadamard gate.
Nb blocks, each with Np parameterized gates, the Hadamard test requires O(NbNp) controlled operations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix D states the circuit it uses and its controlled-gate count.

assertions.value: The authors state that angle update can be further simplified by replacing the indirect measurement with direct ones, which removes the need for the ancillary qubit and the controlled gate (Fig. 4 (c)). They state the cost in Appendix E: the ancilla-free version requires the execution of additional circuits.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II D, p. 4; Appendix E, p. 11
quotes: This removes the need for the ancillary qubit and the controlled gate resulting in the circuit shown in Fig. 4 (c).
We can avoid the use of those while requiring the execution of additional circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix E states the ancilla-free version and the extra circuits it needs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ancilla-based angle update is efficient in terms of circuit depth but still uses an ancilla qubit and a controlled operation which may be challenging to realize on existing hardware.
quotes: angle update is eﬃcient in terms of circuit depth, but still uses an ancilla qubit and a controlled operation which may be challenging to realize on existing hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of the ancilla-based version in Appendix E.

assertions.value: The paper derives, for angle update without ancilla or controlled gates, a closed-form update using two expectations for real time evolution and three expectations for imaginary time evolution, all estimated by direct measurements.
quotes: Putting everything together, Eq. (E1) is maximized in closed form using two
Putting everything together, Eq. (E5) is maximized in closed form using three expectations:
All quantities are estimated by direct measurements, without using ancilla qubits or controlled gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix E derives both closed forms from the shift identity for the gate exp(−iθG) with its generator a Pauli operator.
assertions.reader_inference: The derivation uses the technique of Refs. 52 and 53 for replacing indirect with direct measurements, which the paper cites.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for imaginary time and assuming the change in objective function value is small, information from previous steps can approximately be recycled, bringing the total number of circuits to two, and that the error of this approximation is proportional to the modification of the previous parameter and can be reduced by decreasing τ.
quotes: bringing the total number of circuits to two.
For small values of τ , the error of this approximation is proportional to the modiﬁcation δθd−1 of the previous parameter.
assertions.certainty_reason: An approximate argument stated without a test of the approximation's accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate (Table I) the characteristics of cone, block and angle update along with the tdvp methods of the cited prior work: circuits per sweep are of order the product of the number of blocks in the causal cone and the parameters per block for cone, block and angle update, and of order the square of that product for tdvp; matrix inversion is No for the three update methods and Yes for tdvp; controlled gates per circuit are of order the product for cone update, of order the parameters per block for block update, and of order one for angle update and for tdvp.
assertions.anchor: Table I, p. 5; Sec. III B, p. 5
quotes: TABLE I. Characteristics of cone, block, and angle update along with the tdvp methods of Ref. [16].
O(NbNp) O(NbNp) O(NbNp) O(Nb2Np2)
Matrix inversion No No No Yes
Controlled gates per circuit O(NbNp) O(Np) O(1) O(1)
assertions.certainty_reason: A table of the authors' own cost counts, given without derivation in the text; the tdvp column is their reading of a cited method.
assertions.reader_inference: Nb2Np2 is printed flat by the text layer and reads as the number of blocks squared times the parameters per block squared. The comparison is of asymptotic counts; the paper runs no head-to-head experiment against tdvp.

assertions.value: The authors conclude from the comparison that angle update requires the smallest amount of resources per sweep and no matrix inversion, which they say makes it a stable and efficient algorithm for simulating time evolution, and that block update interpolates between angle and cone update in a natural way.
quotes: We conclude that angle update requires the smallest amount of resources per sweep and no matrix inversion
block update interpolates between angle and cone update in a natural way.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from Table I's cost counts.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I gives angle update the same circuits per sweep as cone update and block update; the smaller figure is the controlled-gate count per circuit.

assertions.value: The authors state that for imaginary time evolution their algorithm significantly reduces the hardware requirements over existing methods and produces accurate ground state approximations, and that for real time evolution they present a hierarchy of algorithms in which the accuracy can be systematically improved by utilizing more hardware resources.
quotes: show that for imaginary time evolution our algorithm signiﬁcantly reduces the hardware requirements over existing methods and produces accurate ground state approximations.
We present a hierarchy of algorithms where the accuracy can be systematically improved by utilizing more hardware resources.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the support is the Table I cost counts and small-system exact simulations.
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment in the paper compares the hardware use of these algorithms with the tdvp methods; the comparison is by operation counts.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing a numerical analysis text, that matrix inversion is numerically unstable when the condition number of the matrix is large and small errors in the matrix can become large errors in the matrix inverse. They state that the tdvp methods of the cited prior work require measurements of order 1/ε² (printed 1/ 2) for a desired accuracy per matrix element.
quotes: Matrix inversion is numerically unstable when the condition number of the matrix is large and small errors in the matrix can become large errors in the matrix inverse [57].
For a desired accuracy per matrix element, this procedure requires O(1/ 2) measurements.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (Golub and Van Loan; Ref. 16).
assertions.reader_inference: The epsilon in the measurement count was lost by the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a desired accuracy in the time-evolved parameters the number of measurements for the tdvp update scales as O(κ2/ 2) in the worst case, where κ is the condition number and the printed exponents are the square of κ and the square of the accuracy; Appendix F derives an upper bound on the relative accuracy of the solution vector B proportional to κ divided by the square root of the number of measurements m, ignoring the product of the two error terms δAδB, with the matrix elements assumed to carry a Monte Carlo sampling error that falls with the square root of the number of measurements.
assertions.anchor: Sec. III B, p. 6; Appendix F, Eqs. (F9)-(F10), pp. 13-14
quotes: We show in Appendix F that for a desired accuracy in the time-evolved parameters the required number of measurements scales as O(κ2/ 2) in the worst case.
where we have used AB = C, ignored δAδB, and where · is a norm.
Equivalently, Eq. (F10) states that for a desired accuracy in B we need the number of measurements m to scale like O(κ2/ 2).
assertions.certainty_reason: A first-order perturbation bound that drops the product of the two error terms and is stated for the worst case, not a proved tight scaling.
assertions.reader_inference: The bound is on the tdvp methods the paper compares against, not on the paper's own algorithms. Exponents and the accuracy symbol were lost by the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the matrix inversion required in the original tdvp methods leads to a computational cost scaling like O(κ2/ 2) for accuracy ε (printed with the symbols lost), and that the additional factor of κ squared compared with the standard measurement error can be computationally challenging, especially for ill-conditioned matrices A.
quotes: We conclude that the matrix inversion required in the original tdvp methods [15, 16] leads to a computational cost scaling like O(κ2/ 2) for accuracy .
Compared with the standard measurement error O(1/ 2) the additional factor of κ2 can be computationally challenging especially for ill-conditioned matrices A.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the Appendix F bound; stated as a worst-case scaling.

assertions.value: The authors report the median condition number of 100 random initializations of their Ansatz, ignoring singular values smaller than 10−7: κ̃ ≈ 16 with 15 parameters, κ̃ ≈ 5001 with 45 parameters, and κ̃ ≈ 17085 with 75 parameters.
quotes: We obtain some numerical evidence by computing the median condition number κ˜ of 100 random initializations of our Ansatz.
To avoid instabilities, we ignore singular values smaller than 10−7.
With 15 parameters we have κ˜ ≈ 16, with 45 parameters we have κ˜ ≈ 5001, and with 75 parameters we have κ˜ ≈ 17085.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study with exact simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say in this passage which matrix the condition number refers to; from Appendix F it is the tdvp matrix A. The parameter counts match the causal cones of Fig. 6 (45 and 75 parameters) and a single block (15 parameters).

assertions.value: The authors state that the rapid increase of the condition number as a function of the number of variational parameters indicates a challenging scaling of tdvp cost for their choice of Ansatz.
quotes: This rapid increase of the condition number as a function of the number of variational parameters indicates a challenging scaling of tdvp cost for our choice of Ansatz.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's interpretation of three measured medians; no scaling law is fitted.
assertions.reader_inference: Three parameter counts do not fix a growth rate.

assertions.value: The paper derives, for a PQC with real parameters, the tdvp equation as a linear system in which the real part of the matrix A (elements Aj,k built from derivatives of the state) times the parameter-velocity vector B equals the imaginary part of the vector C, and states that imaginary time evolution leads to similar systems of linear equations.
quotes: Re(Aj,k)Bk = Im(Cj).
This leads to the ﬁnal tdvp equation:
other applications such as imaginary time evolution lead
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix F derives the equation by minimizing the stated squared distance over real parameter velocities.

assertions.value: The authors state that a pth-order Trotter product formula has an error scaling as O(τ p+1) per time step τ (printed flat, tau to the power p plus 1) for sufficiently small values of τ, and that the total Trotter error for the complete time evolution over N = t/τ time steps scales as O(τ p).
quotes: A pth-order Trotter product formula has an error scaling as O(τ p+1) per time step τ for suﬃciently small values of τ .
Then the total Trotter error for the complete time evolution over N = t/τ time steps scales as O(τ p).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without derivation as a known property of product formulas.

assertions.value: The authors state that there are two sources of error, a Trotter error and a variational error due to the limitations of the PQC Ansatz and optimization methods, that both can be quantified and systematically decreased, and that the variational error can be decreased by adding new blocks to the PQC and performing more optimization sweeps.
quotes: In our methods there exist two sources of error.
Both errors can be quantiﬁed and systematically decreased.
can be decreased by adding new blocks to the PQC and performing more optimization sweeps.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; Fig. 6 shows that block and angle update do not benefit from more sweeps, and only depth 2 was tested.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement that more sweeps lower the variational error is supported in the paper only for cone update (Fig. 6); the paper reports no experiment that adds blocks.

assertions.value: The authors report real time evolution of the zero state under the quantum Ising chain with J = 1, λ = 0.2, n = 6 and t = 2, using cone update with six sweeps, and that the second-order Trotter method resulted in smaller errors than the first-order method for all values of τ tested.
quotes: We perform real time evolution of the |0 state under the quantum Ising chain with J = 1, λ = 0.2, n = 6, and t = 2.
In order to achieve a small variational error we use our most accurate algorithm, cone update, with six sweeps.
The second-order method resulted in smaller errors for all values of τ .
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one exact simulation of one six-qubit system.
assertions.reader_inference: The tested values of τ are given only on the axis of Fig. 5 (the text layer lists 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2); the quotes do not carry them.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the larger values of τ the Trotter error is larger than the variational error, and for the smaller values of τ the variational error accumulates over more time steps and rapidly becomes larger than the Trotter error, consistent with similar studies for matrix product states.
quotes: We observe that for the larger values of τ , i.e., fewer time steps making up the total evolution, the Trotter error is larger than the variational error.
For the smaller values of τ , i.e., more time steps in the entire evolution, the variational error accumulates over more time steps and rapidly becomes larger than the Trotter error.
This observation is consistent with similar studies that were carried out for matrix product states [56].
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation from one simulation of one system.

assertions.value: The authors set up an experiment on the accuracy of cone, block and angle update using the depth D = 2 Ansatz with periodic boundary conditions and randomly initialized parameters, with a time step of 0.1 for cone update, and, for block update, a step of 0.1/(NsNb) and, for angle update, 0.1/(NsNbNp), where Ns is the number of sweeps. The four-qubit causal cone encloses three blocks and 45 parameters; the six-qubit cone encloses five blocks and 75 parameters; the results average over 25 random initial states and random Pauli-product Trotter terms.
assertions.anchor: Sec. III C, p. 7; Fig. 6 caption, p. 6
quotes: We use the Ansatz in Fig. 3 (a) with depth D = 2,
